chunks: "To keep the eye out of the mask I'd work from the specification down to a budget and then verify it with margin.

I start by turning the mask and BER target into budgets: how much of the unit interval and how much of the eye amplitude can be consumed by jitter, ISI, reflections, crosstalk and noise before the mask is hit.

Then I simulate the channel early: extract S-parameters for the traces, vias and connectors, run a statistical or time-domain eye with the real driver and receiver models, including equalization, and see the margin before I lay out the board.

In layout I protect the budget: controlled impedance, length and skew matching, short or back-drilled via stubs, a low-loss material if required, spacing to avoid crosstalk, solid references, and clean, well-decoupled supplies and clock.
Then I measure: eye and mask margin on the prototype, not just pass or fail, across temperature, voltage and several units, with realistic aggressors running.
I want a margin sized from the measured spread across units and corners, not just a pass, to cover production variation.
If the margin is thin, I tune equalization or revisit the worst budget item, and I add stress tests such as injected jitter to see how much headroom remains."
